Female Largescale mullet (Parachelon grandisquamis) reach a maximum standard length of 40 centimeters [Li = 40 centimeters], a size that distinguishes them from many smaller mugilid congeners that typically mature at shorter body lengths. This ultimate total length is achieved after several years of sustained growth in the coastal lagoons and estuarine habitats they frequent along the West African coast. Field surveys have documented that females grow more slowly than males after the onset of gonadal development but ultimately surpass them in maximum size, a pattern linked to the energetic demands of egg production. The species is commercially important across its range, and understanding its growth trajectory is essential for setting appropriate mesh sizes in artisanal fisheries to protect the spawning stock. Growth rings on scales and otoliths have been used to validate this asymptotic length, showing that few individuals exceed the 40 centimeter mark even in unfished populations. Comparative data from the closely related Mugil cephalus suggest that such a maximum length is at the upper end of the typical range for tropical mullets occupying similar trophic niches.

Sexual maturation in this species occurs when individuals attain a total length of 15 centimeters [Lp = 15 centimeters], a threshold that corresponds to the onset of gametogenesis and the first appearance of vitellogenic oocytes in the ovaries. This length at puberty is relatively small compared to the ultimate size, meaning that females begin allocating resources to reproduction well before their somatic growth has ceased. Histological examinations of wild-caught specimens indicate that the initiation of reproductive activity is more strongly correlated with body size than with chronological age, a phenomenon common among teleosts living in variable environments. Juveniles in productive estuaries may reach this length during their first year, whereas those in less favorable habitats may take an additional growing season. The total length at puberty of 15 centimeters [Lp = 15 centimeters] also marks the size at which individuals typically join the adult schooling aggregations that migrate toward spawning grounds. This developmental milestone has implications for fishery management, as catching fish below this size removes individuals that have not yet contributed to the next generation.

The pelagic eggs of Parachelon grandisquamis are small and transparent, with each fertilised ovum having a wet weight of 0.00038 grams [Wwb = 0.00038 grams], a value derived from the average egg diameter of 0.9 millimeters observed in related species of the genus Mugil. This minute mass of each fertilized ovum (0.00038 grams) [Wwb = 0.00038 grams] reflects the high fecundity typical of mullets, which produce large numbers of small yolky eggs that develop rapidly in warm coastal waters. Following external fertilisation during broadcast spawning events, the zygotes drift with the currents for roughly 24 to 48 hours before hatching. The yolk-sac larvae that emerge are lecithotrophic and depend entirely on endogenous reserves until their mouth opens and they begin exogenous feeding approximately three to four days post-eclosion. The modest wet weight of the egg enables females to produce tens of thousands of eggs per spawning event without exhausting their body reserves, an adaptation to the high mortality rates experienced during the early planktonic stages. Comparative data from Mugil cephalus confirm that an egg diameter near 0.9 millimeters represents the lower end of the size spectrum for mugilids.

At the onset of sexual maturity, females achieve a wet weight of 33.8 grams [Wwp = 33.8 grams], a body mass that corresponds closely to the weight predicted from the length-mass relationship established for this species. This weight at puberty represents the point at which females have accumulated sufficient energy reserves to support vitellogenesis and the subsequent spawning migration. Individuals below this mass rarely exhibit signs of gonadal recrudescence, suggesting that a minimum body condition is required before the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis is fully activated. The value of 33.8 grams [Wwp = 33.8 grams] is derived from the standard length-weight equation using the species-specific parameters documented in field studies from the Gulf of Guinea. Once females surpass this threshold, they typically spawn for the first time during the next appropriate hydrological season, which is often linked to the onset of the rainy season and the associated increase in coastal productivity. The relatively modest weight at puberty, in comparison to the ultimate adult weight, illustrates a life-history strategy that prioritizes early reproduction despite the potential trade-off with continued somatic growth.

Fully grown females attain an ultimate wet weight of 611 grams [Wwi = 611 grams], a value estimated from the length-weight relationship for individuals at the maximum recorded total length of 40 centimeters. This asymptotic body mass represents the heaviest individuals documented in wild populations and is typically reached only by females several years old that have completed most of their somatic growth. Under optimal thermal conditions, such as those found in the tropical estuaries of Senegal and Gambia where water temperatures average 26.5 °C [T = 26.5 °C], reproductive output reaches its maximum rate with females producing approximately 4 million eggs per year [Ri = approximately 4 million eggs per year] and spawning approximately once per year [F_R_i = spawning approximately once per year]. This high fecundity is characteristic of mullets and helps offset the substantial egg and larval mortality typical of pelagic spawning. The annual egg production value is derived from studies on the closely related Mugil bananensis and reflects the species' capacity for rapid population turnover, corresponding to a daily reproduction rate of approximately 4 million eggs per year [Ri = approximately 4 million eggs per year]. The combination of large body size and high reproductive investment positions Parachelon grandisquamis as a classic r-selected strategist among coastal marine fishes. Longitudinal studies indicate that the oldest documented individuals in the wild reach a lifespan of 10 years [am = 10 years] when residing in cooler waters averaging 17.5 °C [T = 17.5 °C], though longevity may be reduced in warmer, more productive environments due to accelerated metabolic rates.
